column5: خلق فسوّى; dust formed and breath
column6: The commentary reads خلق فسوّى as a body completed before breath is given. Genesis 2:7 likewise has God form the human from dust and then breathe life into that formed body.

column5: خلق فسوّى; fashioned body and reversal
column6: Job says God's hands fashioned and made the speaker, then asks whether that same maker will destroy him. It gives a personal biblical counterpart both to ordered formation and to the commentary's later reversal of formed life.

column5: womb formation and equal making
column6: Job grounds equal treatment of servant and master in one maker who fashioned both in the womb. This sharpens the commentary's claim that orderly human embodiment includes the hearer, not an abstract creature.

column5: womb body set in order
column6: The commentary opens the womb as a place where an incomplete body is gathered and ordered. Psalm 139:14 says God formed the inward parts and wove the speaker in the mother's womb.

column5: creator and former from womb
column6: Isaiah identifies YHWH by making and forming Israel from the womb. Its action-based divine identification closely matches the relative clause that identifies the Lord through خلق and سوّى.

column5: stretching heaven, founding earth, forming spirit
column6: Zechariah joins the stretching of heaven, founding of earth, and formation of the human spirit. That threefold formula places the commentary's sky, embodied person, and breathed interior in one creator's work.

column5: measured earth and stretched a line
column6: The commentary hears in خلق the measured work that precedes an irreversible cut. Job's creation speech asks who fixed the earth's measures and stretched a measuring line over it, making cosmic order explicitly artisan-like.

column5: waters measured; hills weighed in balance
column6: Isaiah pictures God measuring waters in a hollow hand, marking off heaven, and weighing hills in scales. It supplies a concrete biblical analogue for the commentary's measured creation, balance, water, and completed fitting.

column5: formed earth, made it, established it
column6: Isaiah says the creator formed, made, and established the earth rather than making it empty. Its sequence closely illuminates the commentary's insistence that خلق followed by سوّى is completed ordered creation, not a bare first act.

column5: father made and established Israel
column6: Moses names God by making and establishing Israel rather than by a detached title. This is a close biblical counterpart to the commentary's point that the Lord is known through the actions in a relative clause.

column5: divine speech and immediate coming-to-be
column6: The commentary contrasts a craftsman's material work with creation effected by command. Genesis 1:3 gives the compact pattern of divine speech followed immediately by the existence of light.

column5: spoke, commanded, and it stood firm
column6: Psalm 33 says God spoke and it came to be, commanded and it stood firm. The verbal creation and resulting stability parallel the commentary's reading of creation and completion as one uninterrupted divine work.

column5: bowing before our maker
column6: The surah's praise command is grounded in the Lord's creating action. Psalm 95 calls worshippers to bow and kneel specifically before YHWH their maker, providing the same liturgical logic.

column5: creator alone; heavenly host worships
column6: Nehemiah calls YHWH alone the maker of all the heavens, earth, seas, and their contents, and says the heavenly host worships him. It joins exclusive creation to praise as the commentary does.

column5: praise because he commanded and created
column6: Psalm 148 explicitly orders heavenly creatures to praise because God commanded and they were created. This is an unusually close parallel to praise attached to a creator-relative clause.

column5: creator gives breath and spirit to walkers
column6: Isaiah identifies God as creator and stretcher of the heavens who gives breath to people and spirit to those walking on earth. It links cosmic ordering, formed life, breath, and the commentary's transition from made body toward guided walking.

column5: made earth and established world by wisdom
column6: Jeremiah says God made the earth, established the world by wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by understanding. It supplies a biblical sequence of making, stabilizing, and cosmic proportion.

column5: all things made by the divine word
column6: Wisdom addresses God as the one who made all things by his word. It gives a Jewish formulation for the commentary's contrast between a human cutter's materials and creation by a command.

column5: measure, number, and weight
column6: Wisdom says God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight. Its threefold account of cosmic proportion directly accompanies the commentary's extended claim that خلق already bears measured fitting.

column5: created works assigned their boundaries
column6: Sirach says that when the Lord created his works he determined their boundaries. The verse offers a precise Jewish formulation of measured creation before the later guidance and provision developed in the commentary.

column5: nothing made incomplete; paired order
column6: Sirach describes creation as paired in opposites and says nothing was made incomplete. That is a particularly close parallel to the commentary's سوّى as removing excess and supplying what is lacking.

column5: Creator formed humankind and restores breath
column6: The mother tells her son that the Creator shaped human origins and will give life and breath back. It directly joins the commentary's womb formation, breathed life, and re-creation of a body after death.

column5: morning prayer: created, formed, breathed soul
column6: The daily soul prayer says God created, formed, and breathed the soul into the worshipper. Its ordered verbs make a Jewish liturgical counterpart to the commentary's formed body, breath, and praise of the maker.

column5: formed dust and breathed a speaking spirit
column6: This Targum expands Genesis 2:7's dust-and-breath scene into a living, speaking human. It is a Jewish interpretive elaboration of the commentary's completed bodily form awaiting the imparted spirit.

column5: Torah as an architect's blueprint
column6: The commentary says the creator's measure needs no pre-existing model, unlike a leather worker's pattern. Genesis Rabbah compares creation to an architect using a blueprint and says God looked into Torah, a deliberately different craftsman-image that lets the contrast be assessed.

column5: Abraham exposes powerless hand-made idols
column6: The commentary places Abraham's creator-and-guide confession against crafted idols. Genesis Rabbah's tale of Abraham smashing Terah's idols supplies the major Jewish expansion of that same anti-idol setting.

column5: craftsman measures and shapes a human-like idol
column6: Isaiah's carpenter stretches a line, marks out, and shapes an image for worship. The human measuring and cutting scene mirrors the commentary's artisan imagery while exposing its opposite: an object fabricated as a god.

column5: maker of all things alone
column6: Isaiah identifies YHWH as maker of all things, stretching the heavens and spreading the earth alone. It closely supports the commentary's conclusion that the one who sets the measure needs neither model nor partner.

column5: carved image as teacher of lies
column6: Habakkuk calls a crafted idol and its maker's trust a teacher of lies. This gives a precise biblical analogue for the commentary's secondary sense of خلق as fabricated false speech opposed to the true creator.

column5: gods that made neither heaven nor earth perish
column6: This Aramaic verse declares that gods which did not make heaven and earth will perish from them. It makes the commentary's test between the creator and made idols, including the destructive end of false works, explicit.

column5: heavens and earth wear out like a garment
column6: The commentary traces smoothness into the wearing of a garment and the reversal of formed creation. Isaiah says the earth will wear out like a garment while God's salvation remains, giving the image a cosmic scope.

column5: uneven ground made level for the way
column6: The commentary preserves the destructive edge of سوّى, which can level a settlement, and joins bodily uprightness to a straight path. Isaiah's preparation scene raises valleys, lowers mountains, and makes rough ground level for a way.

column5: potter remakes a spoiled vessel
column6: Jeremiah's potter reworks a spoiled vessel into another as he sees fit. It renders the commentary's maker-and-material image concrete and shows that the one who forms can also re-form what has failed.

column5: bones in the womb and God's work
column6: Ecclesiastes pairs the hidden formation of bones in a pregnant woman with the unknowable work of God who makes everything. It gives a close biblical analogue to the commentary's womb-stage meditation without reducing it to a mechanical account.

column5: grass for cattle and plants for human service
column6: The commentary follows ordered heaven toward water, pasture, and livelihood for people and animals. Psalm 104 says God makes grass grow for cattle and vegetation for human use, matching that provision sequence.

column5: rain makes grass sprout in desolate land
column6: In Job's creation speech, rain satisfies the waste land and causes grass to sprout. It is a direct counterpart to the commentary's movement from ordered creation through water to pasture.

column5: rain waters earth and makes it sprout
column6: Isaiah's rain descends, waters the earth, and brings sprouting, seed, and bread. It closely parallels the commentary's water-to-pasture-to-sustenance chain after creation is set in order.

column5: humankind made upright; humans devise schemes
column6: Ecclesiastes says God made humankind upright but humans sought many devices. The contrast gives a biblical analogue to the commentary's formed balance versus self-devised, false construction.

column5: create a clean heart
column6: The commentary extends ordered formation to the self, guidance, and purification. Psalm 51 asks God to create a clean heart, making inner restoration a fresh creative act.

column5: new heart and new spirit
column6: Ezekiel promises a new heart and spirit in place of a stony heart. It gives a prophetic counterpart to the commentary's movement from shaped self to moral direction and purification.

column5: formed and made for divine glory
column6: Isaiah calls those created, formed, and made for God's glory. It binds human formation to glorification of God's name, the relation that frames the commentary's opening command to praise.

column5: creation grounds a recurring act of worship
column6: The Sabbath command is grounded in God's making heaven, earth, sea, and all within them. It provides a Torah instance where liturgical obedience is explicitly reasoned from complete creation.

column5: world created by ten utterances
column6: Avot says the world was created through ten sayings. This rabbinic formulation develops the commentary's command-and-creation contrast while giving creation a moral and covenantal purpose.

column5: all things came to be through the Word
column6: John says all things came to be through the Word and nothing came to be apart from it. It is a Christian formulation of the commentary's word-like, non-artisanal creation.

column5: worlds framed by God's word
column6: Hebrews says the worlds were prepared by God's word so that what is seen did not arise from visible things. This closely illuminates the commentary's claim that divine creation is not dependent on a prior material pattern.

column5: calls non-existent things into being
column6: In its Abraham-and-resurrection argument, Romans describes God as giving life to the dead and calling non-existent things into existence. It joins the commentary's unprecedented creation to its later resurrection horizon.

column5: all visible and invisible things created
column6: Colossians gathers heaven, earth, visible, and invisible things under creation. It gives a Christian cosmic counterpart to the commentary's deliberately objectless خلق فسوّى, which embraces body and heaven together.

column5: all things hold together
column6: After speaking of creation, Colossians says all things hold together in Christ. This supplies a Christian idiom for the commentary's سوّى as coherence, fitting, and completed order rather than mere origination.

column5: maker of world not housed by human hands
column6: Paul identifies the God who made world and all within it as Lord of heaven and earth, not confined to hand-made temples. It directly accompanies the commentary's creator-versus-human-maker contrast.

column5: giver of life, breath, and all things
column6: Acts says God gives everyone life, breath, and all things. It closely parallels the commentary's formed body followed by imparted breath, while retaining the creator's independence from human service.

column5: divinity unlike art made by human design
column6: Paul rejects likening the divine to gold, silver, or stone shaped by human craft and imagination. The verse provides a direct Christian counter-scene to the commentary's measuring artisan and fabricated deity.

column5: lie exchanges Creator for creature
column6: Romans says people exchanged God's truth for the lie and served a creature rather than the Creator. It precisely matches the commentary's juxtaposition of true creating, fabricated speech, and idolatry.

column5: worship because all things were created
column6: Heavenly worship names God worthy because by his will all things existed and were created. It gives the same rationale as the surah's praise: creation itself warrants liturgical glorification.

column5: worship maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs
column6: Revelation commands worship of the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and water springs. It combines the commentary's praise command, cosmic maker, and life-giving water imagery.

column5: God gives each seed its own body
column6: Paul says God gives a seed a body as he wills, each with its proper body. This is a focused analogy to the commentary's created thing made fit for its particular task and to resurrection re-embodiment.

column5: creation light shines in hearts
column6: Paul invokes the God who commanded light from darkness and applies it to illumination of hearts. It moves the commentary's spoken creation into inward knowing without confusing the two contexts.

column5: new self created for righteousness and holiness
column6: Ephesians calls believers to put on the new self, created according to God in righteousness and holiness. It offers a Christian ethical counterpart to the commentary's formed self, guidance, and purification.

column5: Jesus fashions clay sparrows that fly
column6: The commentary discusses Jesus shaping a bird from clay and insists that life comes by God's permission. The Infancy Gospel of Thomas recounts the closely related clay-sparrow scene, but presents the child Jesus commanding the birds to fly without the Qur'anic permission formula; the difference is interpretively central.

column5: creation wears out like clothing
column6: Hebrews says the heavens and earth will wear out like a garment. It gives a New Testament counterpart to the commentary's worn garment and the decline of what was once smoothly formed.

column5: creation freed from decay
column6: Romans describes creation's bondage to decay and hoped-for liberation. It gives theological depth to the commentary's secondary movement from ordered creation into deterioration and hoped-for renewal.

column5: valleys filled and rough ways made smooth
column6: Luke applies a preparation-for-the-Lord prophecy in which valleys are filled, mountains lowered, and rough ways made smooth. It closely joins the commentary's leveling sense of سوّى to its straight-path and guidance imagery.

column5: not one letter passes from the Law
column6: The commentary contrasts making complete with dropping a letter and connects it to the promise of unfailing recitation. Matthew's saying that not one iota or stroke will pass gives a specific Christian scriptural parallel for that preservation image.

column5: rain, fruitful seasons, food, and joy
column6: Paul describes the living creator's witness through rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness. It is a close Christian analogue to the commentary's route from ordered sky and water to pasture and sustenance.

column5: God as builder of all things
column6: Hebrews uses house-building to say that the builder of all things is God. This directly complements the commentary's artisan analogy while reserving universal creative agency for God.

column5: maker of all things new
column6: The enthroned speaker says, 'I make all things new.' This provides a Christian eschatological counterpart to the commentary's claim that the maker can reverse decay and bring another creation.

column5: Creator established and ordered all things
column6: 1 Clement praises the Creator who established the heavens and arranged creation by incomprehensible understanding. Its early Christian interpretation closely echoes the commentary's sequence from creating to setting in order.

column5: creation work completed and sanctified
column6: Genesis says God blessed the seventh day because he rested from all the creating work he had made. It gives a biblical completion formula beside the commentary's reading of فَسَوّى as the finishing of creation.

column5: perfect work and just ways
column6: Moses calls God's work perfect and all his ways just. It gives an ethical-theological counterpart to the commentary's سوّى as a making free of deficiency and imbalance.

column5: former of all hearts
column6: Psalm 33 calls God the one who forms all hearts and attends to all deeds. It extends the commentary's formed body and soul into an account of inward moral life.

column5: all made for its fitting purpose
column6: Proverbs says YHWH made everything for its purpose. Its purposive language helps articulate the commentary's secondary claim that what is created and measured is made apt for an end.

column5: Spirit makes and divine breath gives life
column6: Elihu says God's Spirit made him and the Almighty's breath gives him life. It is a compact Joban restatement of the commentary's ordered formation followed by enlivening breath.

column5: dust returns; spirit returns to giver
column6: Ecclesiastes says dust returns to earth and spirit returns to the God who gave it. This gives the commentary's formed body and later reversal a mortality-and-return frame.

column5: God leads and makes crooked ground level
column6: Isaiah promises to lead the blind on an unknown way and make crooked places level. It makes the commentary's passage from fashioned uprightness to divinely guided straight way concrete.

column5: song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
column6: The commentary connects complete ordering to the assurance that no recited letter will be dropped. Deuteronomy says the covenant song will not be forgotten from Israel's descendants' mouths, a close Torah memory analogue.

column5: chaff driven away by wind
column6: The commentary's pasture finally becomes dark chaff and its water image distinguishes what remains from what passes away. Psalm 1 contrasts rooted fruitfulness with chaff driven off by wind.

column5: grass withers, word stands
column6: Isaiah juxtaposes withering grass with the enduring divine word. It gives a biblical parallel both to the commentary's pasture-to-waste reversal and to its later concern for preserved recitation.

column5: waterskins of heaven tipped out
column6: Job asks who can count clouds in wisdom and tip the waterskins of heaven. The image belongs beside the commentary's measured leather water-container and rain retained or released from the sky.

column5: water brought from struck rock
column6: The commentary's Arabic خ ل ق B011 image is a hollow in smooth rock that retains water. Exodus reverses the direction: divine action brings water out of the struck rock, making a specific biblical counter-image for rock and life-giving water.

column5: image and likeness in human creation
column6: The commentary emphasizes an unprecedented act that needs no prior model. Genesis frames human creation with the language of divine image and likeness, a different conceptual grammar that matters when comparing formed humanity.

column5: no form seen, therefore no image made
column6: Moses warns that Israel saw no form at Horeb and must not make an image. It gives a Torah anti-idol frame for the commentary's separation of the creator from every fabricated likeness.

column5: source Arabic خ ل ق B008/B006; Hebrew חלק
column6: The commentary's source labels give Arabic خ ل ق the secondary senses of smoothness and allotted share. Isaiah 57:6 plays on Hebrew חלק for the smooth stones of a valley and for one's portion amid offerings to them; the apparent cognacy and its phonology need verification, but the concrete semantic meeting is unusually rich.

column5: source Arabic خ ل ق B006; Hebrew חלק
column6: The commentary uses the source label خ ل ق B006 for a measured share and contrasts worldly and otherworldly portion. Psalm 17:15 speaks of those whose Hebrew חלק is in this life, a likely cognate-based parallel that makes the worldly-share contrast explicit.

column5: source Arabic س و ي; Hebrew שוה
column6: The commentary's Arabic س و ي explores equality, balance, and the maker without equal. Isaiah uses Hebrew שוה in the Holy One's question, 'to whom shall I be equal?'; the proposed Arabic-Hebrew cognacy should be checked, but the source context supplies the same divine incomparability.

column5: God's workmanship created for good works
column6: Ephesians calls believers God's workmanship, created for prepared good works. It offers a Christian ethical development of the commentary's claim that formed things are made suitable for a directed task.

column5: new creation in Christ
column6: Paul calls the person in Christ a new creation. This is an interpretive Christian extension of the commentary's creation-and-recreation language rather than a parallel embryology scene.

column5: Jesus breathes and gives the Holy Spirit
column6: The commentary repeatedly places breath after completed form. In John, the risen Jesus breathes on disciples and gives the Holy Spirit, reusing the breath-of-life pattern in a new-creation setting.

column5: Jesus makes mud and restores sight
column6: The commentary's Jesus scene involves shaping clay and life by divine permission. John has Jesus make mud from earth and apply it to a blind man's eyes for healing, a canonical but differently purposed clay action.

column5: God works miracles through Jesus
column6: The commentary's clay-bird account repeatedly qualifies Jesus' action by God's permission. Acts presents Jesus as attested by miracles that God did through him, a useful New Testament agency formula without claiming the same miracle.

column5: flesh and glory as grass that withers
column6: First Peter compares all flesh and its glory to grass and a flower that wither and fall. It gives a Christian application of the commentary's pasture-to-chaff and formed-life-to-decline imagery.

column5: new self renewed after Creator's image
column6: Colossians describes the new self as renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator. It brings Christian image language into the commentary's themes of formed self, knowledge, and renewed moral direction.

column5: outer person decays, inner person renewed
column6: Paul contrasts the wasting outer person with the daily renewal of the inner person. It offers a concise Christian analogue to the commentary's aging reversal of created form and its inward renewal.

column5: creation seen as wholly very good
column6: The commentary takes فسوّى as creation brought to a complete, balanced condition. Genesis 1:31's judgment that all God made was very good gives a whole-creation counterpart to that completed goodness.

column5: formed in womb and appointed for a task
column6: Jeremiah is formed in the womb before birth and appointed for prophetic work. This joins the commentary's womb formation to its claim that what is measured and made is fitted toward a directed calling.

column5: father, potter, clay, work of divine hands
column6: Isaiah calls God father and potter and the people clay, all the work of his hands. It offers the most explicit Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's maker-and-material imagery without treating the maker as a merely human artisan.

column5: craftsman skillfully shapes a piece of wood
column6: The commentary uses measured cutting and shaping as an analogy that must not be mistaken for divine dependence on a template. Wisdom describes a craftsman's skilled shaping of wood, supplying the human workmanship side of that comparison.

column5: mortal potter fashions a futile god from clay
column6: Wisdom contrasts the mortal, earth-formed potter with the futile god he fashions from clay. This is a direct Jewish counter-scene to the commentary's creator versus fabricated deity and its clay-bird discussion.

column5: potter's control of clay in maker's hand
column6: Sirach compares clay in a potter's hand with human beings in their maker's hand. It gives a Jewish wisdom analogue to the commentary's workmanship image and divine freedom to order or rework what is made.

column5: image is false and has no breath
column6: Jeremiah says the image is false and that there is no breath in it. It exactly joins the commentary's false fabricated speech to its distinction between shaped material and the divine giving of life.

column5: idols are the work of human hands
column6: The commentary contrasts the creator with objects made by craftsmen. Psalm 115 calls idols silver and gold, the work of human hands, giving the classic biblical formulation of that distinction.

column5: a craftsman made the calf, so it is not God
column6: Hosea says the calf came from Israel and a craftsman made it, therefore it is not God. This makes the commentary's test of genuine creating against manufactured worship concrete.

column5: earth returned to waste and lightless disorder
column6: Jeremiah sees the land as waste and void with no heavenly light in a judgment vision. It is a powerful biblical reversal of ordered creation beside the commentary's destructive edge of سوّى.

column5: fruitful land becomes wilderness and cities ruins
column6: Jeremiah's judgment turns fruitful land into wilderness and ruins its cities. It directly parallels the commentary's movement from pasture and formed settlement toward blackened waste and leveling.

column5: new heavens and new earth
column6: Isaiah promises new heavens and a new earth, with the former no longer remembered. It provides a prophetic counterpart to the commentary's claim that the creator can replace a decayed order with another creation.

column5: Spirit creates and renews the face of ground
column6: Psalm 104 says that God sends forth Spirit, creatures are created, and the face of the ground is renewed. It closely combines the commentary's breath, creation, and renewal of earth after decline.

column5: breath enters dead bones and they live
column6: Ezekiel's vision has God promise breath to dead bones so that they live. It is a direct prophetic counterpart to the commentary's formed body, imparted breath, and capacity for re-creation.

column5: maker of hearing ear and seeing eye
column6: The commentary's bodily sequence includes hearing and sight as gifts after ordered formation. Proverbs explicitly names YHWH as maker of both ear and eye, extending the bodily detail into biblical wisdom.

column5: breath withdrawn, creatures die and return to dust
column6: The commentary pairs a once-completed creation with aging and reversal. Psalm 104 says that when God withdraws breath, creatures die and return to dust, giving that reversal an elemental form.

column5: sea receives a fixed boundary
column6: The commentary makes measured limits part of creation before pasture and provision. Proverbs portrays God assigning the sea its boundary and setting earth's foundations, a distinct water-and-measure image.

column5: water wears away stone and washes soil
column6: The commentary's Arabic root imagery moves from smooth rock and retained water to wearing and leveling. Job's waters wear down stones and wash away soil, giving a concrete biblical erosion image for that secondary development.

column5: three partners in human generation and God-given spirit
column6: The commentary treats creation and enlivening as the one creator's action. Niddah 31a distributes parental bodily contributions and God's gift of soul and spirit, a Jewish anthropological counter-model that directly bears on formed body and breath.

column5: source Arabic س و ي; Hebrew שוה amid idol comparison
column6: The commentary's source Arabic س و ي includes equality and the creator's lack of an equal. Isaiah 46:5 uses Hebrew שוה in its challenge about making God equal while its following context concerns goldsmith-made gods; the proposed cognacy requires lexical verification.

column5: hand-made gods lack sensory life
column6: Deuteronomy depicts service to gods made by human hands that neither see, hear, eat, nor smell. It gives an expanded Torah counterpoint to the commentary's claim that crafted things lack the life and agency of their creator.

column5: Creator perceived through things made
column6: The commentary says the highest Lord is recognized in what he does rather than moved away from the world. Romans says God's power and divinity are perceived in the things made, a close New Testament formulation of that logic.

column5: all things sustained by a powerful word
column6: Hebrews describes the Son as bearing all things by the word of his power. It offers a Christian development of the commentary's creation-by-command and its reading of ordered creation as ongoing coherence.

column5: things made by hands are not gods
column6: Paul's Ephesian opponents are said to have heard that gods made by hands are not gods. This is a direct New Testament counterpart to the commentary's rejection of an artifact as a true creator.

column5: all things from the Father and through one Lord
column6: First Corinthians confesses one God, the Father, from whom all things are, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things are. Its twofold Christian creation formula is a significant theological counter-narrative to the commentary's unqualified single-agent formulation.

column5: perishable body raised imperishable
column6: Paul contrasts a body sown perishable with one raised imperishable. It makes the commentary's formed body, decay, and anticipated re-creation into an explicit resurrection contrast.

column5: earth formed through water by God's word
column6: Second Peter recalls heavens of old and earth formed out of and through water by God's word. It supplies a Christian water-and-word creation image beside the commentary's sky, measured water, and earthly provision.

column5: water from the rock given a Christological reading
column6: The commentary develops smooth rock, retained water, and the provision that remains. First Corinthians rereads Israel's wilderness water from the rock as spiritual drink from Christ, a distinct Christian interpretive extension of the rock-and-water image.

column5: chaff burned after the harvest
column6: The commentary's ordered pasture ends as dark chaff in its destructive horizon. Matthew's harvest image separates grain from chaff and burns the chaff, adding an eschatological use of the same agricultural remainder.
